title: The jet that ran out of fuel because of maths
caption:
Air Canada 143, 1983: fuel worked out in pounds instead of kilograms. Both engines stopped at 41,000 ft. ✈️
The captain glided it onto an old air base that was hosting a race day. Nobody was seriously hurt.
Would you have checked the units? Be honest.
first_comment: One unit mix-up, 69 people gliding at 41,000 ft. Pounds or kilograms: which side are you on? ⚖️✈️
sources: Transport Canada / Board of Inquiry (Lockhart report, 1985) into Air Canada Flight 143, 23 July 1983, Boeing 767-200 C-GAUN, Montreal-Ottawa-Edmonton
Fuel was computed with a pounds-per-litre factor (1.77) where kilograms per litre (0.8) was needed: about 22,300 lb (~10,100 kg) on board instead of the 22,300 kg required
Both engines flamed out at about 41,000 ft; most electronic flight instruments went blank; the ram air turbine deployed to power hydraulics

Captain Robert Pearson, an experienced glider pilot, used a forward slip to land on the decommissioned RCAF Station Gimli runway, then in use as a motor-racing strip during a race day; the nose gear did not lock and collapsed; no serious injuries among the 61 passengers and 8 crew
